lesson.title: Building a New Function One Slice at a Time
lesson.summary: The first part of the fundamental theorem says that if F(x) is built by accumulating f from a to x, then F is differentiable and F'(x) equals f(x): differentiating an accumulation function simply hands back the integrand.
lesson.body:
Start with a function f and a fixed point a, and define a brand new function F by letting its input x control how far the accumulation runs: F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt. Notice the letter t inside the integral rather than x. That is deliberate: t is a dummy variable sweeping across the interval of accumulation, while x is the input that decides where that sweep stops. F is a running total, and as x increases, more of f gets folded into the total.

The first part of the fundamental theorem of calculus says that this running total function is differentiable, and its derivative is simply the original function: F'(x) = f(x). Here is why that is believable rather than magical. Compare F(x + h) to F(x) for a small step h. The difference F(x + h) - F(x) is exactly the extra sliver of accumulated area picked up between x and x + h. For h small, that sliver looks approximately like a thin rectangle with width h and height f(x), so F(x + h) - F(x) is approximately f(x) times h. Divide both sides by h and you get the difference quotient [F(x + h) - F(x)] / h, approximately equal to f(x). As h shrinks toward 0, that approximation becomes exact, and the difference quotient is precisely the definition of F'(x). So F'(x) = f(x) falls directly out of comparing accumulated slivers to thin rectangles, the same picture used to build Riemann sums in the first place.

Here is a fully worked example. Let f(t) = t^2 and define F(x) = the integral from 0 to x of t^2 dt. Using the antiderivative rule for powers, an antiderivative of t^2 is t^3/3, so F(x) = x^3/3 - 0^3/3 = x^3/3. Now differentiate this explicit formula directly: F'(x) = d/dx(x^3/3) = 3x^2/3 = x^2. That matches f(x) = x^2 exactly, confirming FTC part one in this concrete case: building the accumulation function and then differentiating it hands back the original integrand, without ever needing to revisit the Riemann sum that originally defined F.

This result depends on the concept of an antiderivative in a subtle but important way: it guarantees that every reasonably well behaved function f actually has one, namely the accumulation function F itself, even in cases where no elementary formula for that antiderivative can be written down. That guarantee becomes especially useful a few chapters ahead, when the derivative of an integral is computed directly for functions whose antiderivatives cannot be expressed in closed form at all.
